patient.name: Joanna Kowalski
patient.complaint: Stabbing electric-shock pains in the right cheek for 6 weeks
background: Takes the combined oral contraceptive pill
No history of multiple sclerosis; no family history
Dentist found nothing wrong last week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with seconds-long, unilateral, electric-shock facial pain triggered by touch, chewing, brushing teeth or cold wind, with a normal examination; a young patient or MS history adds a secondary cause.

points: Joanna, 47: sudden **stabbing** pains in her **right cheek**.
Each lasts **a few seconds**, like an **electric shock**.
Set off by **brushing her teeth**, chewing and cold wind.
Up to 20 attacks a day; she has started skipping meals.

steps.lead: Brief, severe, one-sided pain over Joanna's cheek: the **maxillary (V2)** territory of the trigeminal nerve.
Joanna's attacks are **brief, intermittent, unilateral, electric-shock-like** and set off by innocuous touch: the defining pattern.

steps.q: Which division of CN V supplies Joanna's cheek and upper lip?
steps.r: The **maxillary (V2)** division supplies the cheek, upper lip and upper teeth. V3 supplies the jaw and lower lip; V1 the forehead.

points: Facial sensation and corneal reflexes are **normal**.
Muscles of mastication and facial movement normal.
Hearing normal; eye movements and vision normal.

steps.lead: Joanna's **normal examination** is exactly what classical trigeminal neuralgia should look like.

steps.title: Facial and head pain: trigeminal neuralgia vs mimics
head: Feature
Trigeminal neuralgia

steps.lead: Joanna has no MS history; at 47 her likely cause is **neurovascular compression**, but **MS** must cross your mind in younger patients.

visual.title: Age and the under-40 red flag
visual.label: Joanna 47
visual.caption: Under 40 makes MS or a structural cause more likely.

steps.lead: Joanna has **no red flags**: one-sided, no visual or hearing change, no family history of MS and over 40.

steps.text: 'Pain on chewing' does not mean **giant cell arteritis**. GCA is jaw claudication (aching after chewing) in over 50s; trigeminal neuralgia is a seconds-long electric shock.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is none (clinical diagnosis) in a typical older patient, or MRI brain when the patient is under 40 or has red flags.

steps.q: Joanna is 47 with a typical history and normal examination. What confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: Trigeminal neuralgia is a **clinical diagnosis**. MRI is reserved for young patients or red flags.

steps.lead: Joanna's history and normal exam make the diagnosis; she does not need routine imaging.

steps.title: Does this patient need an MRI?
nodes: Under 40, bilateral, visual or hearing loss, MS family history, deficit?
Yes → MRI brain and urgent referral
steps.caption: MRI looks for MS plaques, tumours or structural compression.

steps.lead: If Joanna were **34**, or her pain were bilateral, an **MRI brain** would look for MS, a tumour or structural compression.

steps.title: Baseline bloods before carbamazepine
steps.text: Normal baseline sodium; useful because **carbamazepine** commonly causes **hyponatraemia**.
In the exam, 'normal neurological examination' plus typical triggers means no scan. Add 'aged 32' or 'history of optic neuritis' and the answer becomes **MRI brain**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' with carbamazepine as the answer, then questions on its side effects (hyponatraemia, contraceptive failure), second-line drugs, and referral for refractory disease or red flags.

steps.q: What is the first-line treatment for Joanna?
steps.r: **Carbamazepine**, a sodium channel blocker. Simple and opioid analgesics do not work well; triptans are for migraine.

steps.lead: Joanna starts **carbamazepine**. She is on the **COCP**, which carbamazepine makes unreliable, and her **sodium** needs watching.

steps.text: Carbamazepine is an **enzyme inducer**. Joanna needs a contraceptive that is not affected, such as a copper IUD or the levonorgestrel IUS, not just 'a stronger pill'.

visual.title: Joanna on carbamazepine
visual.caption: Attacks fall within days to weeks as the dose is titrated.

steps.title: Week 6: she feels muddled and nauseous
steps.text: New **hyponatraemia** on carbamazepine: the classic side effect.

visual.title: Sodium at week 6
visual.label: Joanna 128
visual.caption: Symptomatic hyponatraemia: she is switched to a second-line drug.

steps.lead: Because of her hyponatraemia, Joanna moves to a **second-line** option such as gabapentin, baclofen or lamotrigine (oxcarbazepine also lowers sodium).

steps.title: Trigeminal neuralgia management
nodes: Not tolerated or ineffective → oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, baclofen or lamotrigine

steps.lead: If drugs fail, Joanna can be referred for **microvascular decompression** (moving the artery off the nerve) or **radiofrequency ablation**.
Had Joanna been under 40 or had bilateral pain, she would need an **urgent referral** rather than a prescription alone.
Joanna's care follows **NICE CKS**: carbamazepine first, specialist advice if it fails, urgent referral for red flags.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the artery that compresses the nerve, why light touch triggers pain (demyelination and ephaptic transmission), why MS matters in the young, and how carbamazepine works.

steps.lead: Joanna's likely cause is a loop of the **superior cerebellar artery** pressing on the nerve root where it enters the **pons**.

steps.title: From a pulsing artery to a lightning bolt
nodes: Arterial loop compresses CN V root entry zone
Ephaptic cross-talk: touch fibres excite pain fibres

steps.lead: Brushing Joanna's teeth fires touch fibres that '**cross-talk**' with pain fibres through bare, demyelinated membrane: **ephaptic transmission**.

steps.q: Why is MS more likely in a 30 year old with trigeminal neuralgia?
o: Arterial loops are commoner in the young
Demyelinating plaques at the root entry zone
steps.r: MS plaques can demyelinate the **trigeminal root entry zone**, especially in younger patients.

steps.lead: That is why Joanna's age (over 40) and lack of MS history reassure; in the young, think **MS plaques**.
Carbamazepine **blocks sodium channels**, stabilising Joanna's irritable nerve membrane and stopping the ectopic firing.

technique.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 2 month history of sudden attacks of pain in the left side of her jaw. Each attack lasts a few seconds and feels like an electric shock. They are set off by chewing and by cold wind. Between attacks she is pain-free. Her dentist found no dental cause. Neurological examination is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about facial pain: duration and trigger are the discriminators.
Unilateral V3 territory, seconds-long shocks, innocuous triggers, pain-free between, normal exam.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Trigeminal neuralgia.**

elim: Lasts 15 to 180 minutes, around the eye, with autonomic features.
Constant throbbing pain with a tender tooth; the dentist found nothing.
Jaw claudication is an ache after chewing, not a seconds-long shock.
Dull ache with clicking and jaw tenderness, not shocks.

steps.x: **E. Trigeminal neuralgia.** Rule: seconds + electric shock + innocuous trigger + normal exam = trigeminal neuralgia.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has a 6 week history of attacks of severe pain in her right cheek and upper teeth, lasting a few seconds and occurring up to 30 times a day. Brushing her teeth and eating trigger them. She has lost weight because she is afraid to eat. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Seconds-long attacks triggered by brushing teeth and eating, with a normal exam, are trigeminal neuralgia. Weight loss comes from avoiding meals.

steps.x: Diagnosis of facial pain: duration and trigger decide it.

clues: Brushing her teeth and eating trigger them
steps.x: Seconds-long V2 pain triggered by innocuous stimuli; weight loss from fear of eating; normal exam.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Trigeminal neuralgia.**

elim: Constant facial ache with fever and nasal discharge; she is afebrile.
Attacks last 15 to 180 minutes, behind the eye.
Constant headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.
Follows a shingles rash; burning, constant pain.

steps.x: **E. Trigeminal neuralgia.** Weight loss from avoiding eating is a classic exam clue.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 2 week history of electric-shock pains lasting seconds in her left lower jaw, triggered by talking. practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her facial pain?
practice.e: Trigeminal neuralgia under 40 with a past episode of resolving leg numbness and brisk reflexes suggests MS. Vascular compression is the usual cause in older patients.

steps.x: It asks for the underlying cause, so decide the syndrome, then why she has it.

clues: numbness in both legs that resolved after 6 weeks
steps.x: Trigeminal neuralgia in someone under 40 with a past relapsing-remitting neurological episode and UMN signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gives hearing loss, tinnitus and facial numbness.
Constant, throbbing pain, not seconds-long shocks.

Dull ache, clicking, worse with chewing.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has a 3 month history of brief, stabbing pains in his left chin and lower lip triggered by a light breeze. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. He has no other symptoms.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with trigeminal neuralgia started carbamazepine 6 weeks ago with good pain control. She now has nausea, headache and confusion. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. She is clinically euvolaemic.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
practice.e: Hyponatraemia is a common side effect of carbamazepine and explains nausea, headache and confusion. Normal ALT and glucose exclude the other options.

steps.x: It asks for a cause of new symptoms after a new drug.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hyponatraemia** from carbamazepine (SIADH-like).

elim: ALT is normal.
Glucose is normal.
No focal signs; the sodium explains it.
Pain is controlled and neuralgia does not cause confusion.

steps.x: **B. Carbamazepine-induced hyponatraemia.** Carbamazepine + low sodium = its classic side effect.

glossary.Trigeminal neuralgia: Brief, severe, electric-shock facial pain in the territory of the trigeminal nerve.
glossary.Trigeminal nerve: Cranial nerve V; carries sensation from the face and supplies the chewing muscles.
glossary.CN V: The trigeminal nerve, the fifth cranial nerve.
glossary.V1: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve: forehead, eye and upper nose.
glossary.V2: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve: cheek, upper lip and upper teeth.
glossary.V3: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve: jaw, lower lip, chin and chewing muscles.
glossary.Maxillary: Relating to the upper jaw; the V2 division of the trigeminal nerve.
glossary.Mandibular: Relating to the lower jaw; the V3 division of the trigeminal nerve.
glossary.Multiple sclerosis: Autoimmune demyelinating disease of the brain and spinal cord with relapsing neurological episodes.
glossary.Neurovascular compression: A blood vessel pressing on a nerve, the commonest cause of trigeminal neuralgia.
glossary.Superior cerebellar artery: Artery from the basilar artery whose loop most often compresses the trigeminal root.
glossary.Pons: Part of the brainstem where the trigeminal nerve enters.
glossary.Root entry zone: The point where a cranial nerve enters the brainstem; vulnerable to compression and demyelination.
glossary.Demyelination: Loss of the myelin insulating a nerve, causing abnormal electrical signalling.
glossary.Ephaptic transmission: Abnormal 'cross-talk' where an impulse in one bare fibre triggers impulses in its neighbour.
glossary.Ectopic: Arising in an abnormal place, here nerve impulses starting along a damaged nerve.
glossary.Carbamazepine: Anticonvulsant sodium channel blocker; first line for trigeminal neuralgia.
glossary.Oxcarbazepine: A carbamazepine relative; a second-line option that can also lower sodium.
glossary.Gabapentin: Anticonvulsant used for neuropathic pain; second line for trigeminal neuralgia.
glossary.Baclofen: A GABA-B agonist muscle relaxant; a second-line option for trigeminal neuralgia.
glossary.Lamotrigine: Anticonvulsant sodium channel blocker; a second-line option for trigeminal neuralgia.
glossary.Enzyme inducer: A drug that speeds liver metabolism of other drugs, lowering their levels, such as carbamazepine.
glossary.COCP: Combined oral contraceptive pill; less effective with enzyme inducers like carbamazepine.
glossary.Hyponatraemia: Blood sodium below 135 mmol/L; can cause nausea, headache and confusion.
glossary.SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH: water retention causing low sodium, which carbamazepine can trigger.
glossary.Microvascular decompression: Neurosurgery that moves the compressing artery off the trigeminal nerve root.
glossary.Radiofrequency ablation: Heat lesioning of part of the trigeminal nerve or ganglion to stop pain signals.
glossary.Cluster headache: Severe one-sided pain around the eye lasting 15 to 180 minutes, with tearing and a red eye.
glossary.Giant cell arteritis: Large-vessel vasculitis in over 50s with headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.
glossary.Jaw claudication: Aching jaw pain that builds while chewing, a sign of giant cell arteritis.
glossary.Corneal reflex: Blinking when the cornea is touched; tests V1 sensation and CN VII.
glossary.Optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve causing painful blurred vision; often an early sign of MS.
glossary.Acoustic neuroma: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve, causing hearing loss and sometimes facial numbness.
glossary.Post-herpetic neuralgia: Persistent burning nerve pain after shingles.
